en: [ACT II]
(Evening of the same day.)

Claude's study. A long, narrow room with tall bookcases filled with paperbound octavos; in the center, a desk cluttered with papers on which sits an oil lamp. It is eight o'clock. Claude is seated, reading. A knock at the door.
[SCENE I]
CLAUDE : Who is it?
OSMONDE, offstage : It's me, Papa.
CLAUDE : Come in, my child. (Osmonde enters from the left.) Well now, what is the matter? To begin with, don't you think it isn't very kind to Mother
CLAUDE : to insist on speaking to me alone? (A movement from Osmonde.) What if I asked her to come too, eh?
OSMONDE : In that case I shall leave.
CLAUDE : Osmonde!
OSMONDE : It's precisely about Mother... well, about Mother and me... So, you understand... You see, Papa, I am not happy.
CLAUDE : My darling!
OSMONDE : Oh, not happy at all. The other day at the prayer meeting you said that our happiness is within us.
CLAUDE : You know very well that it is true.

OSMONDE : For me at any rate, it isn't true... it seems to me there is nothing inside me except what makes me suffer. Or if there is anything else, it's so hidden, so... Oh, Mother knows full well that I am not happy, and I believe she resents me for it.
CLAUDE : But what is it that... is there some particular reason?
OSMONDE : It's rather that there is every reason. Forgive me, I am causing you pain right now.
CLAUDE : My darling, you must tell me everything... and why didn't you speak to me sooner? Don't you realize how dreadful this is for me?...
OSMONDE : Please.
CLAUDE : Surely, after all, I ought to be able to see clearly into you... If even the hearts closest to us are impenetrable...
OSMONDE : It must be precisely because I am too close... You ask me why I didn't speak to you sooner. It is very hard for me to answer you.
CLAUDE, bitterly : You didn't trust me, probably.
OSMONDE : Oh, but I do, Papa, it's only you I trust.
CLAUDE : And your mother, Osmonde?

OSMONDE : Mother is someone who never helps you. To begin with, she sits in such judgment on everything one says, everything one does; and for me, it paralyzes me, to such an extent... And you are so busy, you have so many cares, all those miseries to relieve. One always feels like one is stealing you from someone else. And then, obviously, next to everything you see...
CLAUDE : You tell me you have every reason not to be happy.
OSMONDE : I mean that when I look ahead, I see nothing; life has no attraction for me.
CLAUDE : What?

OSMONDE : Yes, to you, life—isn't it?—is a gift from God, something grand, magnificent; Life! when you say that word, your voice trembles. But to me, on the contrary, it seems paltry, insignificant. My life...
CLAUDE : Yet you have before you... (He makes a gesture.)
OSMONDE : Marriage... children... is that what you mean?
CLAUDE : Yes. (A silence.)
OSMONDE : Look around us. Henriette Bellanger, Jeanne Schild... they are married, they have children... I find nothing to envy in those lives. Not merely to envy. Nothing of interest.
CLAUDE : Don't you think it is very superficial to judge as you do?
OSMONDE : They have narrow, difficult lives...
CLAUDE : So that's it?
OSMONDE, nervously : But let me explain... Suppose they are happy, I don't know; that means they have husbands who don't cheat on them...
CLAUDE : My darling!

OSMONDE : Children who grow up without too much trouble, with only three or four illnesses on average each year. No, that holds no appeal for me. I don't see any rhyme or reason in such lives. If mine must be cut from the same pattern...
CLAUDE : But there is no pattern. Each of these lives has its secret beauty.
OSMONDE : Secret, yes, you can say that!
CLAUDE : Its inward uniqueness—one would have to live it to be able to appreciate it.
OSMONDE : Thank you: mine is quite enough for me... all the same, as if they were just copies printed by the thousands, by the millions, like newspapers, like tracts... Yes, that's it, tracts.
CLAUDE : Might there not be a little pride at the bottom of all this?
OSMONDE : You know, without pride...
CLAUDE : To conform to the laws of life, to make them one's own, to will them in one's turn...
OSMONDE : That's just a word. Whether one wills it or not...
CLAUDE : It is not just a word, my darling, it is a great truth. To receive in order to give.
OSMONDE : Receive what? Give what? And anyway, if it's only to pass it on to others who will pass it on in their turn, what is the good of this game? This perpetual race in the fog?
CLAUDE, drawing her to him : Then this distress, deep down, means that you...

OSMONDE : When someone is like me, she ought to be able to find support in the faith of others... Until now, your faith has sustained me, your own faith... But when one is too anguished, that is not enough. Right now...
CLAUDE : So, you have a sorrow?
OSMONDE : Not a sorrow.
CLAUDE : An anxiety?
OSMONDE : Rather.
CLAUDE : Won't you tell me what it is? (Mechanically he has pulled out his watch.)
OSMONDE : You looked at your watch?
CLAUDE : You know very well that I am obliged to go out shortly.

OSMONDE, bitterly : You have too many obligations, Papa... Feeling like one is just a number between the unmarried mother on the Rue de l'Ouest and the paralytic on the Avenue du Maine... if you think that makes confiding any easier... And then, perhaps it's also that you receive too many from everyone... It's almost your profession. It chills me a little.
CLAUDE : But, my darling, come now, you know very well that with you it is completely different.
OSMONDE : Yes, in short, I'm a special edition.
CLAUDE : You sound like your mother.
OSMONDE : Ah, do you think so?
CLAUDE : Yes; besides, when she was your age...

OSMONDE : Well! It won't sound very kind at all, but I confess to you that the thought of marrying even someone like you... someone who had a soul like yours... would terrify me. And then to marry a mediocre man would be even worse. Life is frightening.
CLAUDE : But this anxiety, my darling...
OSMONDE : Oh, I know everything you're going to say to me. You preached a sermon on it last month.
[SCENE II]
THE SAME, EDMÉE
EDMÉE : Someone rang, Osmonde, and you know Félicie has gone out.
OSMONDE : At this hour? Who could it be? (She goes out.) (A silence.)
EDMÉE : Are you going out tonight?
CLAUDE : Yes, but it is too early. Forstmeyer won't be home until ten o'clock.
EDMÉE : The idea of making you come at such an hour...
CLAUDE : He spares himself so little...
EDMÉE : Besides, considering how much interest that conversation will hold...
CLAUDE : There is still a great idea in it.
EDMÉE : Grand words, above all... This union of the Churches... besides, deep down, you don't believe in it any more than I do.
CLAUDE : If we do not believe in it, it certainly will never happen.
OSMONDE, re-entering : It's Eugénie bringing a letter from Uncle Francis for you, Papa.
EDMÉE : Really!
CLAUDE : Is there an answer?
OSMONDE : Eugénie doesn't know. She is furious at being given an errand on a Sunday. (Claude has opened the letter; Edmée reads over his shoulder; she gives a violent start.) What is it, Mother?
EDMÉE : It's not possible!
CLAUDE : Osmonde, would you tell Eugénie that there is no answer. (Osmonde goes out.)
EDMÉE : We cannot take this risk. Have the concierge told that you have gone out... or that I am unwell... whatever you like; but if he comes, don't let him be allowed up.
CLAUDE : That is impossible. What kind of lie would that be?
EDMÉE : You lie to your wife, not to your concierge. And besides, since you really must go out... Claude, he is a sick man.
CLAUDE : Precisely.
EDMÉE : Look, you see very well, he went back to your brother's just now. It's an obsession. He is a madman; I refuse to let him enter here.
CLAUDE : My dear, a little composure.

EDMÉE : Again! Claude, we have taken leave of our senses. But even if I myself consented to receive this man, your duty would be to oppose it. (To Osmonde, who re-enters at that moment.) Leave us for a moment, my child.
OSMONDE : Were you talking about me?
EDMÉE : It has nothing to do with you.
OSMONDE : Papa, you won't repeat what I told you?
EDMÉE : What are these secrets now?
CLAUDE, to Osmonde : It's about this letter I've just received.
EDMÉE : You have no explanations to give.
OSMONDE : You look terribly upset.
CLAUDE : No, no, a bit... embarrassed; your mother and I are not quite in agreement. (Osmonde looks at them suspiciously and exits slowly.)
EDMÉE : You heard me, I refuse to let that man enter this house.
CLAUDE : I am waiting for you to be calm.

EDMÉE : You—when I think that I have never once seen you angry!... (She is in the grip of a kind of nervous trembling.) If you think I don't guess what you are thinking right now! You despise me because I am distraught.
CLAUDE, in a low voice : My dear, but your cross, I bear it with you.
EDMÉE : Claude, you are my husband, you are not a priest.
CLAUDE, in the same voice : What is happening to us here is willed; it cannot be... an accident. Edmée, this trial...
EDMÉE : Always that horrible word!
CLAUDE : We must live through it as Christians.
EDMÉE : You don't have what it takes to live through it as a man.
CLAUDE, softly : Won't you pray with me?
EDMÉE, in a pleading tone : Have them say you aren't here. Osmonde! (She goes out. Claude remains alone; he concentrates in silent meditation, his hands clasp together, a long silence.)
EDMÉE, re-entering : I don't know where she is, I'm going downstairs. (Claude does not answer.) Claude! But why, after all?... Is it for him or for us?

CLAUDE, slowly : If we shrink from this meeting, it will prove... I don't know... that the past is not dead, that we have not overcome it. It would be cowardly... it would not be worthy of us. Come, what are you afraid of?
EDMÉE : Of everything.
CLAUDE : Someone once said: "Fear is the sign of duty."

EDMÉE : You know that is false. Good heavens, you rationalize, you quote maxims. Duty! What has duty got to do with this? Ah, listen! What if all this were really a comedy you are playing to yourself, a kind of pose!...
CLAUDE : A comedy...
EDMÉE : Without your even suspecting it.
CLAUDE : So this is where we are! (Osmonde's voice is heard offstage: "Please do come in, Sir, my father is here, I shall go ask him.")
OSMONDE, entering : Papa, there is a gentleman who would like to see you. (Claude turns pale.)
EDMÉE, her eyes fixed on Claude : This gentleman's name?
OSMONDE : Monsieur Sandier.
EDMÉE : Where were you just now, if you please?
OSMONDE : I just went to say good evening to the little girls upstairs.
EDMÉE : Oh! Well!...
OSMONDE : The gentleman was coming up the stairs when I came back down... I had taken the key, so he came in with me.
EDMÉE : Well then, Claude, are we receiving this gentleman? (A vague gesture from Claude.)
OSMONDE, to Claude : But what is the matter with you?
EDMÉE : Your father isn't feeling quite well.
OSMONDE, going to Claude, tenderly : What is it?
CLAUDE : A kind of dizziness.
OSMONDE : I'll go tell the gentleman that you cannot see him. (A silence.)
EDMÉE : No, let him come in... It is someone your father and I knew in the past. (Osmonde goes out; she can be heard saying: "Sir, if you would please come this way...")
[SCENE III]
THE SAME, MICHEL
(Michel Sandier is a man of forty-five to fifty, tall but stooped; his face is deeply hollowed by illness.)
MICHEL, bowing : Madame... Monsieur... I am embarrassed to present myself at such an unseemly hour.
CLAUDE : My brother had mentioned that we might have the pleasure of seeing you this evening... There is no need, is there, to introduce our daughter? The introduction was made of itself.
MICHEL, turning to Osmonde : Indeed, it was Mademoiselle who...
CLAUDE : I understood that you were only passing through Paris?
MICHEL : Yes, I may leave as early as tomorrow.
EDMÉE, with effort : And you have been here since?...
MICHEL : For a week... But I cannot bear Paris, I cannot breathe here. (A silence.)
CLAUDE : I myself once had great difficulty in getting used to it.
MICHEL : And yet you did not come here directly from the Ardèche?
CLAUDE : No, I first had a parish in the North, at Esquerchin, near Lille.
MICHEL : That must be hell.
CLAUDE : Not at all, those years left us with beautiful memories, didn't they, Edmée?
EDMÉE : That depends...
MICHEL : I imagine Monsieur Lemoyne is not speaking of nature.
CLAUDE : Although those vast, bleak expanses are not without grandeur.
MICHEL : As for me, when I pass through there by train, I pull down the blind.
CLAUDE : The people are very endearing.
MICHEL : Ah?
CLAUDE : My wife and I were witnesses to many touching scenes. Victor Hugo's *Les Pauvres Gens*...

MICHEL : Mademoiselle Osmonde, we are old acquaintances, without your suspecting it. I saw you when you were very small, at the time when I lived in Saint-Loup de Talvas in a large house just above the parsonage. I often came to your parents' house, and I can see you now just as you were then... I passed through Saint-Loup again a few months ago.
CLAUDE : I suppose not much has changed since our time.
MICHEL : They have built a small sawmill that spoils the view. Within ten years, there won't be a single unspoiled landscape left.
CLAUDE : Yet a sawmill...
MICHEL : You see nothing else.
OSMONDE : Then it's just like the gasworks at Fonville-Saint-Vincent. We had a little villa on the cliff; we had an expansive view, but there was a gasometer in the background.
CLAUDE : For my part, I never paid any attention to that gasometer.
OSMONDE : You are fortunate, Papa; you only ever see what pleases you.
MICHEL : Wait now, Fonville-Saint-Vincent—why, I drove through there by car last year. It is between Dieppe and Le Tréport?
OSMONDE : Exactly.
MICHEL : It struck me as dreadful. Dusty cubes of nougat between two fortification embankments. (Osmonde laughs.)
CLAUDE : And yet you enjoyed yourself there, Osmonde.
EDMÉE : Naturally.
OSMONDE : Deep down, one can never really form an opinion of a place except over time, and when I think of Fonville, it is without enthusiasm, I assure you!
MICHEL : That seems to me very true; only memory is real, only memory is truly ourselves.
CLAUDE : We had some very pleasant acquaintances there; and then, after all, the sea... the sea... I am quite astonished at what you say.
EDMÉE : You are very good to take these quips seriously.
MICHEL : Take music, for example—it's the same thing. The immediate impression is almost always deceptive.
CLAUDE : There, I must recuse myself.
MICHEL : Does Mademoiselle Osmonde?...
OSMONDE : I am very fond of music, but I so rarely have the opportunity to hear any.
MICHEL : And you play no instrument? I believe I recall that your mother...
EDMÉE : It has been twenty years since I gave it all up.
MICHEL : You had, if I remember rightly, an excellent Érard on which you...
EDMÉE : We gave it away.
MICHEL : In a life like yours, so absorbed, so full, a piano is a temptation.
EDMÉE : At Esquerchin, we wouldn't even have had room to put it.

MICHEL : That is a pity. (A silence.) Passing back through Saint-Loup de Talvas, I took one or two photographs. (To Osmonde.) This might perhaps interest you, Mademoiselle; you must often have heard talk of that little corner. (He hands Osmonde two or three small photographs.)
